extra.message: The `reset-password` CLI command accepts `new_password` as a command-line argument (`p_rp.add_argument("new_password")`). Command-line arguments are visible in the system process list (e.g., `ps aux`) to all users on the same machine, and they are logged to shell history files (.bash_history, .zsh_history). This exposes the new password in plaintext.

The application configuration has `debug: bool = True` as the default. When debug mode is enabled, FastAPI may expose detailed error traces, stack traces, and the interactive API documentation. In production, this can leak internal implementation details, code paths, and sensitive environment information to end users.

The default database_url contains hardcoded cleartext credentials: 'postgresql+psycopg2://support_desk:support_desk@localhost:5432/support_desk'. If this default is not overridden in production (via environment variable or .env file), the database credentials are exposed in source code and application configuration.

Database connection string contains hardcoded credentials (username:password) in source code: 'postgresql+psycopg2://support_desk:support_desk@localhost:5432/support_desk'. The password 'support_desk' is exposed in plaintext in the configuration file. Anyone with access to the source code or configuration file can read these credentials.

The JWT signing secret_key is hardcoded with a development-only default value 'dev-only-change-me-in-prod-fb7c8c8a5d4f4e9b8a1c2d3e4f5a6b7c'. If deployed to production without overriding this via environment variable or .env file, an attacker who discovers this key can forge arbitrary JWT tokens, impersonate any user, and gain unauthorized access to all endpoints.

The secret_key used for signing JSON Web Tokens (JWT) is hardcoded as 'dev-only-change-me-in-prod-fb7c8c8a5d4f4e9b8a1c2d3e4f5a6b7c' in the source code. While the value says 'change-me-in-prod', there is no enforcement mechanism. Any deployment using this default value allows attackers to forge arbitrary session tokens.

The cookie_secure setting defaults to False, meaning session cookies will be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections. This allows an attacker with network access to intercept session cookies via man-in-the-middle attacks, leading to session hijacking.

The application uses cookie-based authentication (HttpOnly session cookie set by `_set_session_cookie`) but does not implement any CSRF protection mechanism. There are no CSRF tokens, no `Origin`/`Referer` header validation, and the `SameSite` cookie attribute is set to `Lax` (not `Strict`). An attacker can craft a malicious page that, when visited by an authenticated user, performs state-changing actions (e.g., password change, ticket modifications) on behalf of the victim using their session cookie.

The CORS middleware is configured with allow_credentials=True and allow_headers=['*']. While the origin is restricted to a single frontend origin, allowing all headers could permit custom headers (e.g., X-* headers) that bypass security expectations. Combined with allow_credentials=True, this is broader than necessary.

The create_webhook endpoint stores a user-provided target_url without any validation or sanitization. The URL is only stripped of whitespace (payload.target_url.strip()) but not checked against private IP ranges, loopback addresses, or metadata endpoints. When the webhook delivery service processes this URL (via outbound HTTP request), it will send requests to attacker-controlled destinations, enabling Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) against internal services.

The ALLOWED_CONTENT_TYPES allowlist includes 'application/octet-stream', which is a generic binary content type that effectively matches any arbitrary file. Since the content-type is user-provided via the form field (not detected from the file content), an attacker can simply set content_type='application/octet-stream' to bypass content-type restrictions entirely. While the extension check provides a secondary gate, .zip (which can contain executables) is also in the extension allowlist.

The /api/auth/register endpoint allows anyone to create new user accounts without any rate limiting, account lockout, CAPTCHA, or exponential backoff. An attacker can automate bulk account creation to exhaust system resources, fill the database, or create accounts for abuse.

The self-service registration endpoint at POST /api/auth/register takes an organization_name from the request body and, if an organization with that name exists, silently adds the new user to it with no verification. A malicious user can register with the name of any existing organization to join that organization and subsequently view all tickets belonging to that organization (since customer users can see their org's tickets via user_can_view_ticket). There is no domain-based verification, invitation token, or admin approval required.

The self-service registration endpoint at POST /api/auth/register has no rate limiting. An attacker can create unlimited user accounts, exhausting database storage and potentially filling disk space with organizations and users.

The login endpoint at POST /api/auth/login has no rate limiting, account lockout, or progressive delay. The User model has a 'failed_login_count' field (defined in models.py line 144) but it is never read or incremented in the login handler — the field exists but is completely unused. An attacker can attempt unlimited password guesses against any user account.

The login endpoint returns different HTTP status codes and messages for disabled accounts (403 'Account is disabled') vs invalid credentials (401 'Invalid email or password'). While the attacker needs to know the correct password, this still leaks information about account status when credentials happen to be correct.

The /api/auth/password/change endpoint has no rate limiting. While it requires authentication, an attacker who has compromised a session token could rapidly change the victim's password without any throttling. Additionally, a brute-force attack on the current_password field could be performed.

The /api/auth/password/reset/request endpoint has no rate limiting, is fully unauthenticated, and writes token data to a file on disk (emails.log). An attacker can spam this endpoint to: (1) enumerate existing emails via timing side-channel or resource exhaustion, (2) fill disk space by writing to emails.log repeatedly, (3) flood a user's inbox with reset emails.

The password reset request endpoint at POST /api/auth/password/reset/request has no rate limiting. An attacker can repeatedly request password resets for a known email address, flooding the user's inbox with reset emails (if email delivery were enabled) and filling the emails.log file on disk.

The password reset flow writes the reset token in plaintext to a file (`storage_dir/emails.log`) on the server filesystem. The token is logged with the user's email address and a timestamp. If an attacker gains access to the server's filesystem (e.g., through a path traversal vulnerability or misconfigured permissions), they can collect valid reset tokens and reset any user's password.

The /api/auth/password/reset/confirm endpoint has no rate limiting. An attacker can brute-force reset tokens by rapidly submitting requests with different token values. While tokens are hashed, an attacker who obtains a plaintext token (e.g., via the emails.log file that logs tokens in plaintext) could quickly reset the password before the user notices.

The api_update_status endpoint at POST /api/v1/tickets/{ticket_id}/status authenticates via API key, but the authorization check at line 143 only scopes the ticket to the key's organization when key.organization_id is truthy. When an API key has organization_id=None (which is allowed by the APIKey model where organization_id is nullable), an attacker with any valid API key can update ANY ticket's status (to closed or open) regardless of which organization the ticket belongs to. The api_create_ticket endpoint at line 77-79 properly blocks API keys without an organization, but api_update_status lacks this check.

The sla_dashboard endpoint executes an unpaginated query loading ALL matching tickets into memory via db.execute(stmt).unique().scalars().all(). The only filtering is an optional 'since' date parameter with a default of 30 days. For a large deployment with millions of tickets, this query could consume excessive database and application memory resources, leading to denial of service.

The sla_export_csv endpoint executes an unpaginated query loading ALL matching tickets into memory via db.execute(stmt.order_by(Ticket.created_at.desc())).unique().scalars().all(). Like the SLA dashboard, this loads all results without any row limit, creating a memory exhaustion vector.

The SLA CSV export writes ticket subject (t.subject) directly into CSV cells without sanitizing for spreadsheet formula injection. A ticket subject beginning with '=', '+', '-', or '@' would be interpreted as a formula when the CSV is opened in Excel or LibreOffice Calc, potentially executing arbitrary commands.

The escalations CSV export writes the escalation reason (e.reason) directly into CSV cells without sanitizing for spreadsheet formula injection. User-supplied escalation reason text beginning with '=', '+', '-', or '@' would be executed as a formula when the CSV is opened in a spreadsheet application.

The dashboard_summary endpoint loads ALL tickets visible to the staff user into memory via db.execute(stmt).unique().scalars().all() with no pagination or limit, then iterates through every ticket to compute status counts, overdue counts, and unassigned counts. For large datasets, this is an expensive operation that consumes significant memory and CPU.

While the `base_ticket_query` scopes ticket visibility by team/assignment for non-admin staff, the `organization_id` filter parameter is applied on top of this scope. A support_agent from Team A can query tickets assigned to their team AND filter by an organization that belongs to a different team's ticket. While the base query limits team scope, the organization filter can be used to probe which organizations have tickets handled by their team, leaking organization information.

The `description` field from `TicketCreateInternal` is stored directly in the database without sanitization through `sanitize_rich_text()`. If the frontend renders ticket descriptions as HTML (common for rich-text descriptions), an attacker can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript into the ticket description. This payload will execute when any user views the ticket details.
The audit log summary for ticket creation includes the ticket subject which may contain sensitive information.
The _notify helper stores ticket subject as notification body. If notifications table access is not properly scoped, subjects leak.

The CSV export endpoint writes ticket subject (t.subject) directly into a CSV cell without sanitizing for spreadsheet formula injection. Cells beginning with =, +, -, or @ are interpreted as formulas by Excel/LibreOffice. Ticket subjects are user-controlled.

While the `PATCH /{ticket_id}` endpoint allows updating the ticket subject, it does not update the description field. However, indirect stored XSS risk exists because the subject (while stripped) is also not sanitized via `sanitize_rich_text`. More critically, the body fields throughout the ticket system flow from user input to API output without HTML sanitization, relying entirely on frontend escaping which the `text.py` comment contradicts by stating replies are rendered as HTML.

The `body` field from `TicketReplyCreate` is stored directly in the database without being sanitized through `sanitize_rich_text()`. The comment in `text.py` explicitly states that replies are rendered as HTML on the frontend. Since the backend provides no sanitization at the storage layer, an attacker can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript (e.g., ``) into ticket replies that will be rendered unsafely by the frontend, resulting in Stored XSS.

The `body` field from `InternalNoteCreate` is stored directly in the database without sanitization via `sanitize_rich_text()`. Internal notes are rendered as HTML on the frontend (per the comment in `text.py`). An attacker (staff user) can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript into internal notes, which will execute when other staff members view the ticket.
list_users endpoint returns UserOut with email, full_name, role, org/team membership, is_active, last_login_at, created_at for all users.
The WebhookCreated Pydantic schema includes a secret: str field that returns the webhook signing secret in plaintext. Could be captured in API/logs.

The seed.py file creates user accounts with hardcoded passwords 'Password123!' for all demo users. While this is intentional for demo purposes, the seed function could be imported and called from any context, potentially creating accounts with known weak passwords in non-development environments.
Seed function returns demo_api_key and demo_password in stats dict. API key written to disk in demo_credentials.txt.

The rich text sanitizer allows `img` tags with `src` attribute pointing to external URLs, enabling image-based tracking or data exfiltration (e.g., using ``). Also, the allowed tags include `a` with `href` which could be used for open redirects.

The deliver_event function makes synchronous HTTP requests to all active webhooks sequentially without any limit on the number of webhooks. If many webhooks are configured, or if a webhook endpoint is slow/unresponsive, this could block the request handler for an extended period, causing resource exhaustion and denial of service.

The webhook signing mechanism uses `hook.secret_hash` (a SHA-256 hash of the original secret) directly as the HMAC key. Since the hash is stored in the database, anyone with database read access can forge webhook signatures. The HMAC key should be the original plaintext secret, not its hash.
Webhook HMAC uses hook.secret_hash (SHA-256 hex digest) as the HMAC key instead of the original webhook secret.

The `deliver_event` function sends HTTP POST requests to `hook.target_url`, which is a user-configured URL. While URLs must start with http:// or https://, there is no validation preventing requests to internal services (e.g., http://localhost:5432/, http://169.254.169.254/).
Webhook delivery failure response body (up to 500 chars) and full original payload are stored in the database via WebhookDelivery model.

The `copyline` query parameter is directly concatenated into an HTML response without any sanitization or escaping. An attacker can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript by passing a malicious `copyline` parameter.

User-controlled JSON from the request body is used to update the entire `workset` dictionary via .update(). This allows an attacker to override security-critical fields including `is_admin`, `role`, and `credit_limit`.

The `ticket_workset_rebind_029` endpoint initializes a `workset` dict with safe defaults (viewer role, is_admin=False, credit_limit=5000) and then applies ALL user-controlled input from the JSON body via `workset.update(change_set)`. An attacker can set `is_admin=True`, change their `role`, or modify `credit_limit` without any validation.

The ticket_agent_packet_030 endpoint returns hardcoded sensitive values including a 'sync_key' ('tok_live_partner_sync') and a 'tax_ref' (US SSN-like '739-44-1982'). These appear to be production credentials hardcoded in the response.

The API response contains hardcoded values that appear to be sensitive: `"sync_key": "tok_live_partner_sync"` (looks like a live API key/token) and `"tax_ref": "739-44-1982"` (format matches a US Social Security Number). These hardcoded secrets are returned to the caller in every response.
The same endpoint returns 'tax_ref': '739-44-1982' which follows US SSN format (XXX-XX-XXXX). Real PII disclosure endpoint design.
The `lane` query parameter is passed directly to RedirectResponse without validation, allowing an attacker to redirect users to arbitrary external URLs.

The ticket_wire_tally_210 endpoint logs the full request body and the Authorization header, which contains the bearer token used for authentication. This sensitive credential could be exposed in log files accessible to system administrators or attackers who gain access to log storage.
The /ops/wire/ticket-tally-210 endpoint logs the raw Authorization header (containing bearer tokens) at WARNING level.

The full request body and Authorization header (including bearer token) are logged in plaintext via `logger.warning("ops tally body=%s bearer=%s", body, request.headers.get("authorization"))`. This exposes authentication tokens to anyone with access to log files.
The full Authorization header (which contains bearer tokens or other credentials) is logged to the application log in cleartext.

The ticket_vault_stash_232 endpoint stores SSN (social security numbers) and credit card numbers in cleartext JSON files on the filesystem. This is a violation of PCI-DSS and data protection regulations that require encryption of such sensitive data at rest.

The `ref` parameter (from query params or request body) is used directly to construct a file path without sanitization. An attacker can use `../` sequences to write files to arbitrary locations on the filesystem.

The `ticket_vault_stash_232` endpoint derives a filename from user-controlled query parameter `ref` (or the JSON payload's `ref` field) without sanitization. The user controls both the file path and the content written, including hardcoded SSN and credit card data. This is a form of mass assignment where the user controls where data is persisted.

The `ticket_vault_stash_232` endpoint uses a user-controlled `ref` parameter (from query params or request body) to construct a file path without sanitization. An attacker can use `../` sequences to write files to arbitrary locations on the filesystem, potentially overwriting application files or writing webshells.

Sensitive personally identifiable information (Social Security Number and credit card number) is stored in plaintext to the filesystem. The code writes `"ssn": payload.get("ssn", "111-22-3333")` and `"card": payload.get("card", "4111111111111111")` to a JSON file on disk without any encryption. Hardcoded defaults for SSN and credit card numbers are also concerning.
MD5 hash is used to compute a digest of user-controlled input. MD5 is cryptographically broken and vulnerable to collision attacks.
The MD5 hash function is used to compute a digest of user-controlled input. MD5 is cryptographically broken and susceptible to collision attacks.

The `ticket_digest_fold_272` endpoint hashes user-controlled input using MD5, which is a cryptographically broken hash function. MD5 is susceptible to collision attacks and should not be used for any security-relevant operations.
The /ops/digest/ticket-fold-272 endpoint uses MD5 (hashlib.md5) to compute a digest of user-supplied input. MD5 is cryptographically broken.
The `ticket_spool_fan_307` endpoint takes a `count` parameter with no upper bound validation, creating a large list in memory. This could allow denial of service through resource exhaustion.

The ticket_relay_probe_354 endpoint takes a user-controlled 'endpoint' query parameter and passes it directly to urllib.request.urlopen() without any URL validation. An attacker with the ops token can make the server issue HTTP requests to arbitrary internal or external hosts, including cloud metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254), internal services, or other private network resources.

The `ticket_relay_probe_354` endpoint passes a user-controlled `endpoint` parameter directly to `urllib.request.urlopen()` without any validation or allowlisting. An attacker can make the server request arbitrary URLs including internal services (e.g., http://169.254.169.254/ for cloud metadata, http://localhost:5432/ for database).

The `ticket_origin_mirror_368` endpoint reflects the Origin HTTP header directly into the JSON response body and sets it as the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header without validation. An attacker can inject arbitrary content via the Origin header.

The `Origin` request header is reflected back as the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` response header with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. This allows any website to make authenticated cross-origin requests to this endpoint, bypassing the Same-Origin Policy.

The Access-Control-Allow-Origin header is set to the request's Origin header value (echoed back) with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials set to true. This allows any arbitrary website to make credentialed cross-origin requests to this endpoint.
The /ops/origin/ticket-mirror-368 endpoint reflects the Origin header back in Access-Control-Allow-Origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.

The `ticket_origin_mirror_368` endpoint reflects the Origin request header as the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` response header and sets `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. This allows any external website to make authenticated cross-origin requests to the application, reading the response.
The `fragment` query parameter is concatenated directly into a Jinja2 template string and rendered. This allows Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI), enabling Remote Code Execution on the server.

The ticket_jinja_cast_378 endpoint takes a user-controlled 'fragment' query parameter and passes it directly to a Jinja2 Template() constructor for rendering. An attacker can inject Jinja2 template expressions (e.g., {{ config.__class__.__init__.__globals__['os'].popen('id').read() }}) to achieve server-side code execution.

The `fragment` query parameter is user-controlled and directly concatenated into a Jinja2 template string which is then rendered via `Template("Result: " + fragment).render()`. This allows Server-Side Template Injection, which can lead to Remote Code Execution through Jinja2's template language (e.g., `{{ config.__class__.__init__.__globals__['os'].popen('id').read() }}`).

The `ticket_jinja_cast_378` endpoint concatenates a user-controlled `fragment` parameter directly into a Jinja2 template string. Jinja2 supports executing arbitrary Python code through template expressions like `{{ config.__class__.__init__.__globals__['os'].popen('id').read() }}`.

The `fragment` query parameter is concatenated directly into a Jinja2 template string and rendered. This allows an attacker to inject arbitrary Jinja2 template expressions. While the immediate result is XSS (since the output is `HTMLResponse`), SSTI can also lead to Remote Code Execution via Jinja2 sandbox escapes. The template is created with `Template("Result: " + fragment).render()` which parses user input as template syntax.
The `name` query parameter is used directly as a filename in a path write operation without sanitization. An attacker can write arbitrary binary content to any location on the filesystem.
The `ticket_dock_shelf_387` endpoint writes binary data to a file whose name is controlled by a user-supplied query parameter `name` with no sanitization or path validation.

The `ticket_dock_shelf_387` endpoint uses a user-controlled `name` query parameter to construct a file path without sanitization. An attacker can include `../` sequences to write arbitrary content to any location on the filesystem.
The `host` query parameter is concatenated directly into a shell command string passed to os.system(). An attacker can inject arbitrary shell commands via shell metacharacters.

The ticket_nonce_roll_408 endpoint uses random.choice() (a non-cryptographic PRNG) to generate codes instead of secrets.choice(). Python's random module uses Mersenne Twister, which is predictable if an attacker can observe enough outputs. This code is used for generating security-sensitive values.
The /ops/nonce/ticket-roll-408 endpoint generates a 'code' using random.choice() which uses predictable Mersenne Twister instead of secrets.choice().
The Python `random` module (Mersenne Twister) is used for generating codes instead of `secrets` module. `random` is predictable and should not be used for security-sensitive token generation.

The ticket_mongo_lane_418 endpoint takes user-controlled JSON and passes it directly as a MongoDB query filter without any validation or sanitization. An attacker can craft MongoDB operators ($where, $ne, $regex, $gt, etc.) to extract data from the MongoDB database beyond what was intended.

User-controlled JSON payload is passed directly as a MongoDB query filter without sanitization. An attacker can inject MongoDB operators (`$where`, `$regex`, `$ne`, etc.) to manipulate the query and potentially access unauthorized data or execute JavaScript on the MongoDB server.

User-controlled JSON payload is passed directly as a MongoDB query filter without sanitization. The `filter` key from the request body (or the entire payload) is used as a MongoDB query, enabling NoSQL injection attacks.
The /ops/mongo/ticket-lane-418 endpoint passes user-supplied JSON as raw MongoDB query filter with no sanitization.
The MongoDB connection string defaults to `mongodb://localhost:27017` with no authentication. If `MONGO_URL` is not set, the application connects to an unauthenticated MongoDB instance.

The `ticket_mongo_lane_418` endpoint creates a MongoDB client and executes a user-controlled query against it. The MongoDB URL is read from the environment, but the endpoint allows arbitrary queries to be executed against the database. Additionally, a user-controlled `filter` parameter is passed directly to `find_one()`, enabling NoSQL injection and arbitrary document retrieval.
SSL certificate verification is explicitly disabled using `ssl._create_unverified_context()` when making HTTPS requests. This allows man-in-the-middle attacks on the outbound connection.

The `ticket_trust_drift_428` endpoint creates an unverified SSL context using `ssl._create_unverified_context()` to make HTTPS requests, disabling certificate validation and enabling man-in-the-middle attacks.

The endpoint makes an HTTPS request with SSL verification disabled (ssl._create_unverified_context()). This disables certificate validation, making the request vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks.

The function grants elevated access ('lead' lane with payroll and casework access) based on the `ops_badge` cookie value, which is fully controlled by the client. Any user can set `Cookie: ops_badge=lead` to gain elevated privileges. This is a classic client-controlled security decision vulnerability.
The endpoint returns internal environment configuration details including the APP_ENV environment variable and the base export directory path.
The /ops/trace/ticket-panel-448 endpoint returns APP_ENV environment variable and BASE_EXPORT_DIR filesystem path in the response body.
Test database DSN contains plaintext password: 'postgresql+psycopg2://support_desk:support_desk@localhost:5432/support_desk_test'

The API client uses credentials: 'include' for cookie-based session authentication, but no CSRF tokens are included in any API request. All state-changing operations (POST, PATCH, DELETE) are performed with the user's session cookie but without any CSRF protection token. If the backend does not implement CSRF protection (e.g., via SameSite cookies or token validation), an attacker could trick an authenticated user into performing unintended actions.

The KB article body is rendered using React's dangerouslySetInnerHTML, which sets innerHTML directly from the server-provided content. Although the comment on line 29 claims the server sanitizes HTML with 'bleach', this is a defense-in-depth bypass at the client side: if the bleach sanitization is incomplete, misconfigured, or has a known bypass (e.g., bleach allowlist gaps allowing event handlers like onload, or newer HTML5 features), this becomes a stored XSS vector. The frontend provides no secondary sanitization or content-isolation mechanism (such as DOMPurify or sandboxed iframe) as a fallback.

The password reset token is read from URL query parameters (params.get('token')). Tokens passed in URLs can leak through Referer headers when the page loads external resources, through browser history, through server access logs, and through shoulder surfing. While password reset links are commonly distributed via email with tokens in URLs, this exposes the token to multiple leakage vectors before the user submits the form.

The ticket API endpoint `/tickets/${id}` is called without any role-based filtering and the full response object (likely containing `internal_notes`, `escalations`, `audit` data) is returned to all users regardless of role. While the frontend UI conditionally renders these sections only for staff (using `{staff && ...}` conditionals), the data is still fully present in the API response. Any non-staff user can view internal notes, escalations, and audit history by inspecting the API response in browser dev tools or by making direct API calls.

The application displays API error messages directly to users via `setError(err.message)` and renders them as `{error}` in the UI. Multiple catch blocks (lines 43, 65, 79, 89, 97, 105, 122, 131, 142, 163, 173, 183) pass `err.message` to `setError`. If the backend API returns verbose error messages containing stack traces, database internals, SQL queries, or path information, these internal details would be exposed to users.

The `is_internal` parameter is set entirely by the client-side checkbox state and sent to the server as a form field. While the checkbox UI is conditionally rendered only for staff (line 298), the actual parameter value is always sent based on `internalUpload` state. A non-staff attacker who manipulates the HTTP request can set `is_internal: 'true'` for their attachment uploads. If the backend trusts this client-controlled parameter to determine whether the attachment should be restricted to staff-only visibility, this constitutes a reliance on untrusted input for a security decision, allowing customers to bypass attachment access controls and potentially upload attachments that are visible only to staff (or vice versa).

The attachment deletion endpoint `/attachments/${attId}` is called with only the attachment ID, derived from the API response. While the frontend UI shows a delete button only for the attachment uploader or staff (line 286-288), the actual API call at line 129 does not verify that the attachment belongs to a ticket the user has access to. If the backend does not independently verify ownership, any authenticated user could delete arbitrary attachments by enumerating IDs.

The grantSlaException function (line 176) sends extend_hours to the backend as Number(slaExtendHours) with NO client-side bounds validation. The HTML input field (line 356) uses `min="1" max="720"` attributes, but these are only enforced by the browser's native form validation — trivially bypassed with browser dev tools or by sending a raw HTTP request. The slaExtendHours state is set from `e.target.value` (line 357), which is a raw string from user input. Number() conversions of negative strings (e.g., Number('-24') = -24), zero (Number('0') = 0, Number('') = 0), or excessively large values are sent directly to the backend. If the backend trusts this value without validation, an attacker can manipulate SLA deadlines in either direction.

The audit log table displays IP addresses (`r.ip_address`) of all actors who interacted with the ticket. While audit logging is a standard security practice, exposing raw IP addresses directly in the UI to all staff users could leak PII (Personally Identifiable Information). IP addresses can be used to infer user location, organization network details, or enable user tracking across different tickets or systems.

The useEffect hook in TicketList.jsx triggers an API call to `/tickets` on every dependency change, and the `search` state (updated on every keystroke at line 79) is in the dependency array. This means each keystroke in the search input dispatches a new API request to the backend. Rapid typing, pasting long text, or automated keystroke injection could cause a flood of backend requests, potentially leading to denial of service. The `alive` flag prevents stale state updates but does not throttle or cancel in-flight requests — new requests are dispatched regardless of pending ones.

The ticket list endpoint `/tickets` is queried with user-controlled filter parameters (`status`, `priority`, `team_id`, `assigned_to_id`, `category_id`, `search`, `overdue_only`, `unassigned_only`). If the backend does not automatically scope the query to only return tickets the current user is authorized to see, this endpoint could leak tickets belonging to other organizations, teams, or users. The frontend simply passes whatever filters are selected, with no tenant or user-scoping enforced.

The CSV export endpoint `/api/tickets/export.csv` is called with user-controlled filters and the resulting CSV is downloaded. If ticket fields (subject, organization name, etc.) contain values starting with `=`, `+`, `-`, or `@`, and the backend does not sanitize these before writing to the CSV, formulas can execute when the CSV is opened in spreadsheet applications like Excel or Google Sheets. This is a classic CSV Formula Injection (CWE-1236) pattern where user-generated content in ticket fields can be weaponized as spreadsheet formulas.

The `downloadFromUrl` function displays error messages from the backend via `alert(err.message)`. The error message is constructed from the response body text (`await res.text()`), which if the backend returns verbose error pages with stack traces or internal details, would be displayed directly to the user via a native alert dialog.
